entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The service-level agreement (SLA) is a formal document outlining the expected level of service between a service provider and a customer. Emerging prominently in the late 20th century, particularly with the rise of the information technology sector, SLAs have become crucial in defining expectations, responsibilities, and quality metrics across various industries. The concept gained traction as businesses increasingly relied on third-party services, notably in telecommunications and IT, where clarity in service delivery became paramount. Figures such as Robert Kahn and Vinton Cerf, pioneers in network protocols, set the stage for the need for standardized agreements due to the growing complexity of networked services.

The formalization of SLAs led to significant developments in service management practices. By the 1980s and 1990s, organizations began adopting SLAs to ensure accountability and performance measurement, particularly in IT services, where uptime and response times became critical metrics. For instance, in 1994, the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) published guidelines that influenced SLA frameworks within internet service provision, establishing benchmarks for reliability and customer satisfaction. The implementation of SLAs not only improved service reliability but also catalyzed the growth of the outsourcing industry, as businesses sought to enhance their operational efficiency while relying on external providers.
